title: Protests for Germany’s car industry as job losses loom
gist: Germany's automotive industry is facing simultaneous demand collapse (European auto sales down from ~18 million in 2019 to ~13 million in 2025), 25% US tariffs, Chinese competition, and a struggling Porsche unit that forced Volkswagen Group to write down $11.5 billion, prompting VW to accelerate workforce cuts and Mercedes-Benz to warn of plant closures, while IG Metall union workers protested at Audi, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, and VW.

themes.theme: Structural decline in European auto demand and German competitiveness

insights.claim: Total automotive sales in Europe fell from a peak of almost 18 million in 2019 to around 13 million in 2025, with an increasing share going to new Chinese entrants, which themselves have spare production capacity to worry about.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A roughly 28% decline in European auto sales over six years is a major structural demand shock for German automakers' home market, directly pressuring their profitability and justifying the capacity-reduction moves described in the article.
insights.locator: Total automotive sales in Europe have fallen

insights.claim: German car makers face simultaneous pressures: declining domestic demand, stronger competition from China, new US tariffs of 25% (subject to change), an aging workforce, and a slow recovery from COVID, on top of the shift to electric vehicles.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Frames a convergence of multiple simultaneous headwinds (not a single cause) facing German auto, useful for investors assessing the sector's risk as compounding rather than transient.
insights.locator: But those companies are now facing multiple problems at once

insights.claim: US tariffs on car exports currently stand at 25 percent and could be subject to change at any time, even though the US market has always been the most profitable market for German car exports.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A 25% tariff on the historically most profitable export market for German automakers is a direct, quantifiable margin headwind, and its stated volatility ('could change at any time') adds material forward earnings uncertainty.
insights.locator: that was before the imposition of new import tariffs

insights.claim: Volkswagen Group is considering closing four of its German factories, news that emerged earlier in summer 2026 and was described as something that would have been 'unthinkable just a few years ago.'
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Potential closure of four German VW factories marks a historic inflection point for a company long considered a pillar of German industrial employment, a significant regional-economic risk signal.
insights.quote: something that would have been unthinkable just a few years ago
insights.locator: Earlier this summer, news emerged that Volkswagen Group

insights.claim: Porsche, majority-owned (75%) by VW Group since 2008, bet too heavily and too soon on the EV transition, building more EVs than it could sell, causing its profit margin to fall below that of the budget brand Skoda; VW Group wrote down $11.5 billion (€10 billion) on Friday, of which $6.9 billion (€6 billion) was attributable to its Porsche stake.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A quantified $11.5B total write-down, with $6.9B specifically tied to Porsche's EV overcapacity, is a concrete, material financial impact directly attributable to premature/oversized EV betting — a cautionary data point for evaluating other premium automakers' EV transition risk.
insights.locator: That’s partly why VW Group had to write down

insights.claim: VW brand head Thomas Schaefer said the 2024 cost-cutting measures agreed with unions were insufficient and that VW would 'significantly step up' its performance program given the likelihood of a 'terrible 2026.'
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Direct executive confirmation that prior restructuring was inadequate and further, larger cuts are imminent signals VW's 2026 outlook is worsening, not stabilizing, relevant for anyone tracking VW's cost structure and earnings trajectory.
insights.quote: I had hoped that the measures agreed in 2024 would already be sufficient. Unfortunately, that has not been the case. We have absolutely no time to lose and will therefore significantly step up our performance program
insights.locator: Faced with the likelihood of a terrible 2026

insights.claim: Mercedes-Benz became the latest OEM to warn workers it might have to close one German assembly plant and one German powertrain plant unless it can achieve cost savings.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Confirms the plant-closure risk is not isolated to VW but spreading industry-wide to Mercedes-Benz, reinforcing the systemic nature of the German auto sector's crisis.
insights.locator: Today, Mercedes-Benz became the latest OEM

insights.claim: Workers protested at Audi, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, VW, and their suppliers, led by IG Metall union head Christiane Benner, who called on corporate leaders to take responsibility for Germany as an automotive nation, for employees, and for jobs.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Coordinated labor protests across nearly all major German OEMs signal rising labor-relations and political risk for the sector as job cuts accelerate, a factor relevant to assessing restructuring execution risk and potential strike/disruption exposure.
insights.quote: We expect corporate leaders and management teams to take responsibility for Germany as an automotive nation, for employees and for jobs
insights.locator: Workers were out in protest yesterday
